content: 1. The evidence from one randomized controlled trial (RCT) was downgraded by one level due to imprecision, as the confidence interval (CI) crossed both the line of no effect and the threshold for a significant benefit. This indicates uncertainty in the results. 2. Data on critical outcomes such as condomless sex, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and the number of sexual partners were not reported. Similarly, accuracy measures like specificity were also not reported. 3. Drug resistance, including the number of cases of HIV mutations related to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), was not reported, which is an important consideration. 4. The number of false negatives, when compared to standard-of-care testing methods, was not reported, which limits the ability to assess diagnostic accuracy. 5. Two subgroup meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate PrEP continuation as prescribed and PrEP continuation as desired. These analyses followed the guidelines outlined in the WHO Handbook and the Cochrane Review manual for addressing clinical heterogeneity. 6. One trial, the JiPime–JiPrEP RCT, was analyzed for PrEP continuation based on adherence over a six-month follow-up period. However, only one RCT was identified for this outcome, leading to a downgrade by one level due to inconsistency. 7. Two studies, the Empower RCT and the PrEP-PP RCT, were pooled to assess PrEP continuation based on adherence. These studies were conducted by Davey et al. (2022) and Mujugira et al. (2022). 8. The risk of bias was downgraded by one level according to the RoB 2 analysis due to missing outcome data in the PrEP-PP RCT. 9. Inconsistency was downgraded by two levels due to substantial statistical heterogeneity (I-squared = 91%) between the Empower RCT and the PrEP-PP RCT. 10. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to a wide confidence interval that included no effect and crossed the threshold for a large effect. An additional downgrade was applied because the total number of participants was fewer than 200 across the PrEP-PP RCT and Empower RCT. 11. No social harms were reported in two studies that examined this outcome. In the Empower RCT, no social harms were reported in either the HIV self-testing (HIVST) arm (0/57) or the standard-of-care (SOC) arm (0/53). Similarly, in the PrEP-PP RCT, no social harms were reported in either the HIVST arm (0/53) or the SOC arm (0/53). 12. Inconsistency in defining social harms was noted. For example, the Empower RCT did not clearly define social harms, whereas the JiPime–JiPrEP RCT defined them as verbal, physical, or emotional abuse by a sexual partner. Additionally, the timing of social harm assessments was unclear in the Empower RCT, unlike the JiPime–JiPrEP RCT, which measured social harms at three months of follow-up. 13. Only one RCT (JiPime–JiPrEP, six-month follow-up) observed social harms, making it impossible to calculate an I-squared value for heterogeneity. This led to a two-level downgrade for inconsistency. 14. Imprecision was downgraded by one level due to a wide confidence interval that included no effect and crossed the threshold for a large effect. This applied to the PrEP-PP RCT, Empower RCT, and JiPime–JiPrEP RCT. 15. Only three RCTs reported HIV incidence results over the trial period: the Empower RCT, JiPime–JiPrEP RCT (12-month follow-up), and PrEP-PP RCT. 16. The risk of bias was downgraded by one level due to incomplete outcome data and differences in the measurement of HIV incidence follow-up periods. For example, the PrEP-PP RCT measured HIV incidence at one month, while the other two RCTs (JiPime–JiPrEP and Empower) measured outcomes at 12 months. 17. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level due to differences in the measurement periods for HIV incidence. However, the I-squared value was 0%, suggesting low heterogeneity. 18. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to a wide confidence interval that included no effect and crossed the threshold for a large effect. The absolute effect ranged from 183 to 1000 more cases per 1000 participants. 19. PrEP implementation and fidelity were not reported, which is an important limitation. 20. Two studies were pooled for HIV testing uptake. However, only one study (JiPime–JiPrEP, six-month follow-up) reported individual HIV testing, and only one study (PrEP-PP RCT) reported partner HIV testing. 21. The risk of bias was downgraded by two levels. The first downgrade was due to incomplete outcome data and selective reporting of partner testing at one-month follow-up. The second downgrade was due to incomplete data from loss to follow-up and bias from partner testing being self-reported by participants rather than their partners. 22. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to a wide confidence interval that included no effect and crossed the threshold for a large effect. 23. Only one RCT (JiPime–JiPrEP, six-month follow-up) was included for individual HIV testing. Three studies were not pooled due to non-individual partner testing or substantial clinical heterogeneity in HIV testing frequency and follow-up. 24. The risk of bias was downgraded by one level due to missing outcome data in the PrEP-PP RCT and unclear risk in the ROBINS-I analysis for Wagner et al. (2022), which lacked a linked published manuscript and relied only on a poster abstract. 25. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level because only one RCT (JiPime–JiPrEP, six-month follow-up) was identified for individual HIV testing uptake. 26. Only one study (PrEP-PP RCT) reported partner HIV testing, leading to a one-level downgrade for inconsistency. 27. The risk of bias for partner testing was downgraded by two levels. The first downgrade was due to incomplete outcome data and selective reporting at one-month follow-up. The second downgrade was due to loss to follow-up and bias from partner testing being self-reported by participants rather than their partners. 28. Imprecision was downgraded by one level due to a wide confidence interval that included no effect and crossed the threshold for a large effect. An additional two-level downgrade was applied due to the low number of participants (<100) in the PrEP-PP RCT. 29. Evidence from the PrEPARE study, a controlled before–after study, was downgraded due to unclear risk of bias, lack of randomization, and reliance on a poster abstract without a linked peer-reviewed publication. The study was not adequately powered to measure differences in PrEP initiation. 30. Inconsistency was downgraded by one level because only one controlled before–after study (PrEPARE) existed for PrEP initiation. 31. Imprecision was downgraded by two levels due to the very low event rate for PrEP offers in the study. 32. Publication bias was strongly suspected, as the evidence was derived from an abstract rather than a peer-reviewed publication. This led to a two-level downgrade.
